screens.title: Exception Handling and Interrupts
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what interrupts, traps, faults, and aborts are, how hardware detects them, and how a processor safely transfers control to a handler and then resumes execution. Exceptions are the mechanism that lets hardware and software cooperate when something unusual happens: an external device needs attention, a program requests a system call, memory is missing, or a fatal hardware error occurs. We'll follow the full sequence the processor performs: detecting the event at a pipeline stage, saving the program counter and status, masking further interrupts, finding the handler in the vector table, executing the handler, and finally restoring state and returning. You will see why precise exceptions matter — why the operating system must know exactly which instruction caused the problem — and how pipelined and out-of-order designs use different hardware structures, like pipeline flushing and the reorder buffer, to preserve precise state. A concrete example we will revisit is a divide-by-zero fault: the processor traps the fault, saves the PC, invokes a page-fault or divide handler in the OS, and then either fixes the condition or aborts. By the end of the module you should be able to explain each step, reason about handler addresses, and evaluate the cost of exceptions on different processor designs.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Exception Handling and Interrupts

Exception Handling and Interrupts

Understand how processors detect exceptional events, save CPU state, transfer control to handlers, and return so execution can safely continue. This matters for OS correctness, performance, and virtualization.

In this lesson
Detection, state save, handler transfer, return.
Coming up
Pipelines, ROB, nested exceptions.
Hands-on
Write a small handler and trigger a divide-by-zero in a simulator.
Concept Map
Events → Save state → Vector → Handler → Return
Quick topics
Interrupts: asynchronous hardware events (timer, I/O)
Traps & Faults: synchronous results of instructions
Pipelines & ROB: ensure precise state

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide what you should be able to explain and do after this chapter. First, you will learn to distinguish interrupts, traps, faults, and aborts: each has a different cause and return address semantics. Knowing this helps you decide who handles an event and whether an instruction can be retried. Second, you'll describe the full exception handling mechanism: detection, precise state save, masking further events, vector lookup, handler execution, and return. That sequence is central to operating-system control and to writing correct handlers. Third, you'll understand the exception vector table and how the processor calculates handler addresses from a base register. This explains why handler code must be placed and aligned carefully. Finally, you'll analyze how exceptions affect pipelined and out-of-order processors, including pipeline flushes and the role of the reorder buffer in providing precise exceptions. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual that relates the concept to an everyday metaphor so you remember the flow and why exact state matters.

screens.title: Exception categories: interrupts, traps, faults, aborts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the four categories used throughout this chapter and highlight the practical difference that matters to an OS. An interrupt is an asynchronous event caused by external hardware, for example a timer tick, keyboard input, or a network packet arrival. Because interrupts originate outside the instruction stream, the processor can delay handling until the current instruction completes; the return address typically points to the next instruction. A trap is a synchronous, intentional transfer initiated by executing a specific instruction — system calls and explicit breakpoint instructions are traps. Traps transfer control to the OS to provide a service, and the return address points to the instruction after the trap. A fault is a synchronous, unintentional event produced by an error during instruction execution: page faults, divide-by-zero, or illegal instructions. The faulting instruction may be restartable; for faults, the return address usually points to the faulting instruction so the OS can fix the condition and retry. Finally, aborts are severe errors where program state is unreliable and the processor cannot safely continue. A concrete example is a divide-by-zero fault: the execute stage raises the fault, the OS can either deliver an exception to the process or terminate it. A common misconception is to treat all exceptions as identical — the return-address semantics and restartability differ and that changes handler design. Think: is the event external or generated by the instruction? That question determines much of the handler's work.

keyIdea.title: Definitions matter
keyIdea.text: Classify events by origin and restartability; that classification determines how the OS handles and resumes execution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Exception categories
Interrupt
Asynchronous hardware event

Caused by external devices; can be masked and often handled after the current instruction completes.

Example: timer tick that schedules the OS to run another thread.
Trap
Synchronous, intentional

Raised by an instruction requesting OS service. Return address points to the next instruction so the program resumes after the trap.

Example: system call instruction invoking a kernel routine.
Fault
Synchronous, unintentional

Occurs when an instruction fails due to an error and may be restartable. The return address often points back to the faulting instruction.

Example: page fault when memory must be loaded from disk.
Abort
Severe, non-recoverable

Hardware-level failure that makes program state unreliable; recovery is usually impossible.

Example: double fault or catastrophic hardware error.
Key Takeaway

Ask whether an event is external or instruction-generated and whether it is restartable; that determines handler semantics and return address.

Common mistake

Treating all exceptions as identical leads to wrong return behavior and possible state corruption.

Try this

For a given event, write whether the OS should retry the instruction or resume at the next instruction and why.

screens.title: The exception handling sequence
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the canonical steps the processor performs when an exception occurs. Step one is detection: hardware logic in a pipeline stage recognizes an exceptional condition — decode may detect illegal instructions, execute sees divide-by-zero, and memory stages detect page faults. Step two is saving processor state: the C P U records the program counter, the processor status register, and any other necessary architectural state. This save can be to a protected stack or to dedicated registers so the handler can restore later. Step three disables further interrupts to prevent nested saves from corrupting the saved context; an interrupt mask bit in the status register is typically set. Step four is vector lookup: the processor uses the exception type as an index into the exception vector table; the table base register plus an entry offset yields the handler address. Step five executes the handler — part of the operating system — which services the event, for example by loading a missing page or performing a system-call service. Step six is return-from-exception: a special instruction restores saved state and resumes execution at the correct return address. A common misconception is that handlers can be treated like normal functions: handlers run with masked interrupts and must explicitly restore machine state using return-from-exception instructions. Practice mapping each step to the hardware signal or register you would inspect to verify it happened correctly.

keyIdea.text: Each step has a precise hardware or software action; handlers are not ordinary functions and must restore masked state with a return-from-exception instruction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Handling sequence
1 — Detect
Hardware observes an exceptional condition in a pipeline stage.

Example: execute stage detects divide-by-zero; memory stage detects page fault.

2 — Save state
PC, PSR, and architectural registers are stored to allow later resume.
3 — Mask interrupts
Set the interrupt-disable bit to avoid nested corruption while saving context.
4 — Vector lookup
Calculate handler address from the vector table base and exception number.
5 — Execute handler
OS code services the event, e.g., fetch page, complete system call.
6 — Return
Return-from-exception restores saved state and resumes at the proper address.
Key Takeaway

Each stage of handling has a verifiable hardware action; treat handlers as privileged sequences that must restore saved state explicitly.

Pro tip

When debugging, log the saved PC and PSR to confirm the exact trap point and interrupt mask state.

Check your understanding

List which pipeline stage would detect three different exceptions: illegal opcode, page fault, and divide-by-zero.

screens.title: Saving processor state
screens.narratorSegment: Saving the processor state is the essential bridge between an asynchronous event and safe handler execution. The hardware must capture the program counter so the system knows where to resume, and it must preserve the processor status register, which contains flags and the interrupt mask. In addition, certain architectural registers may need to be saved or marked as not-yet-committed so the handler can run in a clean context. Processors implement this in one of two ways: writing state to a privileged stack, or saving to special purpose registers. The saved set must be sufficient so that a return-from-exception instruction can restore all visible architectural state exactly. A concrete example is a page fault: the processor saves the PC and PSR, then the handler loads the missing page into memory. After the handler adjusts page tables, it executes the return-from-exception instruction, which restores PC and PSR and lets the C P U restart the faulting instruction. A common misconception is that register windows or speculative state are automatically preserved; in many pipelines, speculative results must be squashed and only committed state is restored. The key is that the saved context must capture everything the OS will need to resume precise, in-order execution.

keyIdea.title: State to save
keyIdea.text: Save PC, PSR, and any architectural state needed to fully restore execution so the OS can retry or continue safely.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Saving processor state
What to save
  • Program Counter (PC)
  • Processor Status Register (PSR) including interrupt mask
  • Architectural register file or indicators of committed state
Where to save

A privileged stack or special registers dedicated to exception context. The mechanism must be atomic with masking so state is not corrupted by nested events.

Example: page fault flow

Memory stage detects a page fault, CPU saves PC and PSR, jumps to page-fault handler, handler loads page, then return-from-exception restores saved state and restarts the faulting instruction.

Common mistake

Assuming speculative register updates are preserved. Uncommitted speculative state must be discarded or never made architectural until commit.

Key Takeaway

The saved context must let the OS restore the architectural state exactly as if instructions executed in order; missing pieces break precise exceptions.

screens.title: Exception vector table
screens.narratorSegment: The exception vector table is the directory the C P U consults to find which routine should handle each exception type. Architecturally it is an array of handler addresses, with one entry per exception number — entry zero typically holds reset, followed by NMI, timer, system call, page fault, and so on. The table's base address is held in a special register, for example the IDT on x86 or VBAR on some ARM implementations. When an exception occurs the processor forms the handler address by adding the exception number times the entry size to the base address. This simple calculation explains practical constraints: the table must be placed in memory the C P U can access in privileged mode, aligned and sized so entries are computed correctly. A concrete consequence is that a misconfigured base register or an incorrectly formatted table entry points the C P U to the wrong handler, causing unpredictable behavior. An important nuance is that some architectures allow per-exception vectoring or fixed vectors, and some architectures let handlers be chained. A common misconception is that handlers are located by name or symbol; in hardware they are just addresses computed from the base and index. When designing an OS or bootloader, ensure the vector table is initialized early and that handlers are safe to call with masked interrupts and a minimal saved context.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Exception vector table
What it is

An array of handler addresses indexed by exception type. The processor computes address = base + exception_number * entry_size.

Example entries: reset, NMI, timer, system call, page fault, divide-by-zero.
Why base register matters

The base register stores the table address; it must be initialized and accessible only in privileged mode to prevent malicious redirection.

Practical checks
  • Confirm base register value at boot
  • Ensure table entries contain valid privileged addresses
  • Respect alignment and entry-size conventions
Common mistake

Assuming vector entries are auto-filled or protected from user-space — ensure privilege separation and correct initialization.

Key Takeaway

The vector table is a simple arithmetic lookup; correct base and entry layout are critical to direct exceptions to the right handler.

screens.title: Exceptions in a simple 5-stage pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: In a basic five-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback) multiple instructions are in flight simultaneously. When an exception is detected in stage N, the processor must ensure precise exceptions: no effects from instructions after the excepting instruction become visible. The hardware strategy is straightforward: flush instructions in stages N+1 through writeback so their results are not applied. Detection logic must exist in each stage that can raise exceptions appropriate to that stage: decode flags illegal opcodes, execute flags divide-by-zero, memory flags page faults. The processor then prevents any writeback from flushed instructions and saves the PC of either the faulting instruction (for faults) or the following instruction (for traps). A concrete scenario: a divide-by-zero detected in execute causes the pipeline to flush the younger instructions that entered fetch and decode; any speculative register updates are prevented from reaching the architectural register file. A typical misconception is that only the fetch stage needs to be stalled; in truth, exceptions can originate in many stages, so detection and coordinated flush must be staged across the pipeline. The key is: the pipeline maintains the illusion of sequential execution by flushing or stalling until the precise exceptional state is restored and the handler completes.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline precision
keyIdea.text: Detect exceptions at their pipeline stages and flush younger instructions so architectural state reflects only committed instructions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › 5-stage pipeline
Stage detection

Different stages detect different exceptions: decode, execute, memory. Each stage's logic can raise a signal that begins the handling sequence.

Flushing

If an exception is detected in stage N, stages N+1..WB are flushed so no younger instruction commits its results.

Concrete example

A divide-by-zero in EX flushes MEM and WB instructions that followed. The saved PC corresponds to the excepting instruction so the OS can decide to abort or retry.

Common misconception

Believing only fetch needs stalling. In fact exceptions can come from later stages and require flush coordination across the pipeline.

Key Takeaway

Precise exceptions require the pipeline to flush younger instructions so only effects from committed instructions become visible.

Try this

Draw a five-stage timeline showing where an exception raised in EX will cause flushes and which PC is saved for a fault versus a trap.

Pro tip

When simulating exceptions, ensure your model prevents writeback from flushed instructions to emulate precise exceptions correctly.

screens.title: Out-of-order processors and the Reorder Buffer (ROB)
screens.narratorSegment: Out-of-order processors execute instructions speculatively and complete them out of program order for performance. Because of this, exceptions cannot be handled by simply flushing later stages: some younger instructions may have finished execution earlier than older ones. The reorder buffer provides the mechanism for precise exceptions: it holds speculative results until instructions are committed in program order. If an exception occurs, the processor discards all uncommitted entries in the ROB and restores the architectural state to the last committed point, leaving the excepting instruction as the next to be handled. The ROB thus prevents speculative side effects from becoming visible before instructions are safe to commit. A concrete example: imagine instruction I causes a page fault while subsequent instructions J and K have already executed out of order and updated temporary buffers; the ROB ensures that I's fault will be presented to the OS while J and K's changes are not applied to the register file or memory. A common misconception is that out-of-order hardware cannot produce precise exceptions; in reality, the ROB is the hardware structure that preserves program-order commitments and enables precise recovery. The key takeaway: the ROB isolates speculation until commit, which is what allows correct exception semantics in aggressive cores.

keyIdea.title: ROB purpose
keyIdea.text: The ROB buffers speculative results and commits them in order so the processor can roll back to a precise state when exceptions occur.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Out-of-order & ROB
Speculation vs. commit

Execution can complete instructions early, but results are held in the ROB until they are safe to commit in program order.

Exception handling

On exception, the ROB flushes uncommitted entries and restores architectural state to the last committed instruction so the OS sees a precise state.

Concrete scenario

Instruction I faults while later instructions J and K have speculatively executed. The ROB prevents J and K from committing; the OS handles I with a consistent state.

Common misconception

Believing out-of-order execution removes the need for precise state. Without the ROB, the OS would observe inconsistent register and memory changes.

Key Takeaway

The ROB is the hardware guarantee that speculative execution won't corrupt architectural state when exceptions occur.

screens.title: Nested exceptions and saved contexts
screens.narratorSegment: Nested exceptions occur when a new exception arises while the processor is already executing an exception handler. To support nested exceptions the processor must save the handler's context as well — effectively stacking contexts so each level can be restored later. Implementations commonly use a dedicated exception stack or multiple banks of saved state to hold nested contexts. Most hardware supports only a limited number of nested levels to avoid exhausting resources; practical designs might allow two to four nested contexts. A concrete example is an NMI fired while servicing a page fault: the processor saves the handler's PC and PSR, switches to the NMI handler, and later returns to the original handler when the NMI is handled. A common misconception is that nesting is unlimited; if too many exceptions nest, the stack or banked registers can overflow, producing an abort or a double fault. The OS and handlers must be written with this limit in mind: handlers typically run with minimal work, re-enable only safe interrupts if at all, and avoid deep recursion so that nested exception depth stays small. Consider this when designing robust handlers: minimize work in handlers, and plan for the limited nested context capacity.

Most hardware supports only a limited number of nested levels to avoid exhausting resources; practical designs might allow two to four nested contexts. A concrete example is an NMI fired while servicing a page fault: the processor saves the handler's PC and PSR, switches to the NMI handler, and later returns to the original handler when the NMI is handled. A common misconception is that nesting is unlimited; if too many exceptions nest, the stack or banked registers can overflow, producing an abort or a double fault. The OS and handlers must be written with this limit in mind: handlers typically run with minimal work, re-enable only safe interrupts if at all, and avoid deep recursion so that nested exception depth stays small. Consider this when designing robust handlers: minimize work in handlers, and plan for the limited nested context capacity.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Nested exceptions
How nesting works

The processor saves the current handler's context and switches to the new handler context. Saved contexts are stacked in a protected area or in banked registers.

Implementation limits

Hardware usually supports a small fixed number of nested levels to avoid resource exhaustion.

Concrete example

An NMI during a page-fault handler causes the OS to save the handler's state, run the NMI handler, then restore and continue the original handler.

Common misconception

Assuming infinite nesting. In practice, nested depth is limited and handlers must be careful not to require deep re-entrancy.

Key Takeaway

Design handlers to be small and predictable; assume only a few nested contexts and avoid deep re-entry to prevent double faults.

screens.title: Maskable interrupts vs non-maskable interrupts (NMI)
screens.narratorSegment: Maskable interrupts and non-maskable interrupts (NMIs) are both mechanisms for external events, but they serve very different purposes. A maskable interrupt can be disabled by clearing an interrupt-enable bit in the processor status register; this allows the C P U or OS to delay handling until it is convenient. Maskable interrupts are used for routine hardware events like timer ticks, keyboard input, and network packets where occasional delay is acceptable. Conversely, a non-maskable interrupt cannot be disabled and is used for critical events that must be acted on immediately, such as memory parity errors, power-failure signals, or watchdog expirations. NMIs generally trigger emergency diagnostic or shutdown procedures because they indicate severe hardware conditions. A concrete example: a watchdog timeout fires an NMI to force immediate attention even if interrupts were disabled. A common misconception is to overuse NMIs for convenience; because they cannot be masked, NMIs complicate handler design and recovery. The handler for an NMI typically must be minimal and robust, performing emergency logging, state capture, or controlled shutdown rather than routine work. When designing systems, reserve NMIs for truly urgent conditions and rely on maskable interrupts for normal device-driven work.

Maskable interrupt

Can be disabled by the interrupt-enable bit. Suitable for routine devices where latency can be tolerated.

screens.title: Writing a minimal exception handler (exercise)
screens.narratorSegment: This activity outlines a minimal handler you can implement in an assembly environment or simulator. The handler must do four things: save the current PC and status register to a stack, print or signal the exception type, restore the saved registers, and execute the return-from-exception instruction. The hands-on exercise suggested in the chapter uses RISC-V, x86, or ARM, but the sequence is the same across architectures. Start by reserving a privileged stack area for exception contexts. In the handler, push PC and PSR, optionally push a small register set the handler needs, then perform a simple output — for example, call a console print routine — and finally pop saved registers and execute the return-from-exception instruction. The main program should deliberately trigger a divide-by-zero to cause a fault. In a simulator like QEMU you can run the program and observe the PC before the exception, the handler PC after vectoring, and the PC after return. If you cannot run a simulator, draw the pipeline timeline showing detection in EX, flushing of later stages, state save, vector transfer, handler execution, and return. A common misconception is to treat the handler like a normal function; remember to use the privileged return-from-exception so the C P U restores masked bits and the exact saved PC.

keyIdea.text: Implement a handler that saves PC/PSR, reports the exception, restores state, and returns; trigger with a divide-by-zero and trace the PCs.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Handler exercise
Handler steps
  1. Save PC and PSR to exception stack
  2. Optionally save required registers
  3. Signal or print the exception type
  4. Restore registers, PSR, PC and execute return-from-exception
Note: use the architecture's return-from-exception instruction so masked bits and privileged state are restored correctly.
Pseudocode assembly
  ; Exception handler entry (pseudocode)
  PUSH  PC        ; save program counter
  PUSH  PSR       ; save processor status register
  PUSH  R0..Rn    ; save minimal registers if needed

  POP   R0..Rn
  POP   PSR
  POP   PC

Handlers must save and restore the exact context and return with the privileged return instruction; treat them as privileged code, not regular functions.

Record the PC values: before the exception, handler entry, and after return. Verify the return PC matches the expected restart point.

If no simulator

screens.title: Virtualization and exception redirection
screens.narratorSegment: Virtualized systems add a layer of decision: should an exception be delivered to the guest OS or trapped to the hypervisor? The chapter presents two mechanisms. Trap-and-emulate intercepts exceptions in the virtualization layer and emulates the expected behavior for the guest, giving the hypervisor full control at the cost of software overhead. Hardware virtualization extensions create root and guest modes so the processor can route certain exceptions directly to the hypervisor (root mode) while others are delivered to the guest. This redirection reduces overhead by letting the hardware handle context switching between guest and hypervisor when necessary. A concrete example: a privileged instruction executed by a guest that would normally trap to the OS may instead trap to the hypervisor so it can emulate or forward that effect. A common misconception is that virtualization removes the need for exception handling in the guest; instead, it changes which layer handles which events. When designing virtual machines, configure which exceptions are intercepted and which are passed through to reduce unnecessary traps while preserving isolation and correctness. The essential point is that virtualization requires careful mapping of exception sources to the right handler — guest or hypervisor — to balance performance and correctness.

keyIdea.text: Decide whether exceptions should be handled by the guest OS or intercepted by the hypervisor to trade correctness and isolation against virtualization overhead.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Virtualization
Trap-and-emulate

Hypervisor intercepts exceptions and emulates behavior for the guest. Simple but can be costly in software traps.

Hardware virtualization

Processor provides root and guest modes so exceptions can be routed to the hypervisor or to the guest with hardware support, reducing overhead.

Concrete example

A privileged guest instruction that would trap to an OS may instead trap to the hypervisor for emulation or shadowing, depending on virtualization configuration.

Design tradeoff

Intercepting more exceptions improves isolation but increases overhead; passing exceptions to the guest reduces hypervisor work but requires safe hardware support.

Key Takeaway

Virtualization adds a routing decision: choose which exceptions the hypervisor intercepts and which are delivered to the guest to balance performance and correctness.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three compact ideas you should carry forward. First: classification — interrupts are asynchronous hardware events, traps are intentional synchronous transfers, faults are synchronous errors that may be restartable, and aborts are unrecoverable hardware failures. Second: handling sequence — detection, saving PC and PSR, disabling interrupts, vector table lookup, handler execution, and return-from-exception. Each step must be reliable so the OS can recover or retry. Third: precise exceptions — pipelined and out-of-order processors require specific hardware strategies: pipelines flush younger instructions, and the reorder buffer ensures that speculative execution does not corrupt the architectural state. These three ideas explain why exception design is both a hardware and an OS concern. Keep them in mind when you write handlers or reason about correctness in complex cores. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what interrupts, traps, faults, and aborts are, how hardware detects them, and how a processor safely transfers control to a handler and then resumes execution. Exceptions are the mechanism that lets hardware and software cooperate when something unusual happens: an external device needs attention, a program requests a system call, memory is missing, or a fatal hardware error occurs. We'll follow the full sequence the processor performs: detecting the event at a pipeline stage, saving the program counter and status, masking further interrupts, finding the handler in the vector table, executing the handler, and finally restoring state and returning. You will see why precise exceptions matter — why the operating system must know exactly which instruction caused the problem — and how pipelined and out-of-order designs use different hardware structures, like pipeline flushing and the reorder buffer, to preserve precise state. A concrete example we will revisit is a divide-by-zero fault: the processor traps the fault, saves the PC, invokes a page-fault or divide handler in the OS, and then either fixes the condition or aborts. By the end of the module you should be able to explain each step, reason about handler addresses, and evaluate the cost of exceptions on different processor designs.

These objectives guide what you should be able to explain and do after this chapter. First, you will learn to distinguish interrupts, traps, faults, and aborts: each has a different cause and return address semantics. Knowing this helps you decide who handles an event and whether an instruction can be retried. Second, you'll describe the full exception handling mechanism: detection, precise state save, masking further events, vector lookup, handler execution, and return. That sequence is central to operating-system control and to writing correct handlers. Third, you'll understand the exception vector table and how the processor calculates handler addresses from a base register. This explains why handler code must be placed and aligned carefully. Finally, you'll analyze how exceptions affect pipelined and out-of-order processors, including pipeline flushes and the role of the reorder buffer in providing precise exceptions. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual that relates the concept to an everyday metaphor so you remember the flow and why exact state matters.

Now that you've seen the high-level goals, this second objectives slide ties each skill to a hands-on or analytic task. For classification, practice by listing an event and deciding whether it is asynchronous or synchronous and whether the return address is the faulting instruction or the next one. For the handling sequence, map each step to hardware actions you can observe: an exception detected in execute or memory stage, registers saved to a stack or special register, interrupts masked, and a table lookup to find the handler. For vector tables, inspect how the base register plus an index produces the handler address — this is a small arithmetic step that explains why table alignment matters. For pipeline analysis, compare a simple five-stage pipeline that flushes later stages with an out-of-order core that relies on a reorder buffer; in practice, you will reason about whether an exception forces many instructions to be discarded and how the OS regains precise state. Each objective closes with a small verification: draw the flow, write the handler pseudocode, and explain the difference between maskable interrupts and NMIs.

Let's define the four categories used throughout this chapter and highlight the practical difference that matters to an OS. An interrupt is an asynchronous event caused by external hardware, for example a timer tick, keyboard input, or a network packet arrival. Because interrupts originate outside the instruction stream, the processor can delay handling until the current instruction completes; the return address typically points to the next instruction. A trap is a synchronous, intentional transfer initiated by executing a specific instruction — system calls and explicit breakpoint instructions are traps. Traps transfer control to the OS to provide a service, and the return address points to the instruction after the trap. A fault is a synchronous, unintentional event produced by an error during instruction execution: page faults, divide-by-zero, or illegal instructions. The faulting instruction may be restartable; for faults, the return address usually points to the faulting instruction so the OS can fix the condition and retry. Finally, aborts are severe errors where program state is unreliable and the processor cannot safely continue. A concrete example is a divide-by-zero fault: the execute stage raises the fault, the OS can either deliver an exception to the process or terminate it. A common misconception is to treat all exceptions as identical — the return-address semantics and restartability differ and that changes handler design. Think: is the event external or generated by the instruction? That question determines much of the handler's work.

This screen walks through the canonical steps the processor performs when an exception occurs. Step one is detection: hardware logic in a pipeline stage recognizes an exceptional condition — decode may detect illegal instructions, execute sees divide-by-zero, and memory stages detect page faults. Step two is saving processor state: the C P U records the program counter, the processor status register, and any other necessary architectural state. This save can be to a protected stack or to dedicated registers so the handler can restore later. Step three disables further interrupts to prevent nested saves from corrupting the saved context; an interrupt mask bit in the status register is typically set. Step four is vector lookup: the processor uses the exception type as an index into the exception vector table; the table base register plus an entry offset yields the handler address. Step five executes the handler — part of the operating system — which services the event, for example by loading a missing page or performing a system-call service. Step six is return-from-exception: a special instruction restores saved state and resumes execution at the correct return address. A common misconception is that handlers can be treated like normal functions: handlers run with masked interrupts and must explicitly restore machine state using return-from-exception instructions. Practice mapping each step to the hardware signal or register you would inspect to verify it happened correctly.

Saving the processor state is the essential bridge between an asynchronous event and safe handler execution. The hardware must capture the program counter so the system knows where to resume, and it must preserve the processor status register, which contains flags and the interrupt mask. In addition, certain architectural registers may need to be saved or marked as not-yet-committed so the handler can run in a clean context. Processors implement this in one of two ways: writing state to a privileged stack, or saving to special purpose registers. The saved set must be sufficient so that a return-from-exception instruction can restore all visible architectural state exactly. A concrete example is a page fault: the processor saves the PC and PSR, then the handler loads the missing page into memory. After the handler adjusts page tables, it executes the return-from-exception instruction, which restores PC and PSR and lets the C P U restart the faulting instruction. A common misconception is that register windows or speculative state are automatically preserved; in many pipelines, speculative results must be squashed and only committed state is restored. The key is that the saved context must capture everything the OS will need to resume precise, in-order execution.

The exception vector table is the directory the C P U consults to find which routine should handle each exception type. Architecturally it is an array of handler addresses, with one entry per exception number — entry zero typically holds reset, followed by NMI, timer, system call, page fault, and so on. The table's base address is held in a special register, for example the IDT on x86 or VBAR on some ARM implementations. When an exception occurs the processor forms the handler address by adding the exception number times the entry size to the base address. This simple calculation explains practical constraints: the table must be placed in memory the C P U can access in privileged mode, aligned and sized so entries are computed correctly. A concrete consequence is that a misconfigured base register or an incorrectly formatted table entry points the C P U to the wrong handler, causing unpredictable behavior. An important nuance is that some architectures allow per-exception vectoring or fixed vectors, and some architectures let handlers be chained. A common misconception is that handlers are located by name or symbol; in hardware they are just addresses computed from the base and index. When designing an OS or bootloader, ensure the vector table is initialized early and that handlers are safe to call with masked interrupts and a minimal saved context.

In a basic five-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback) multiple instructions are in flight simultaneously. When an exception is detected in stage N, the processor must ensure precise exceptions: no effects from instructions after the excepting instruction become visible. The hardware strategy is straightforward: flush instructions in stages N+1 through writeback so their results are not applied. Detection logic must exist in each stage that can raise exceptions appropriate to that stage: decode flags illegal opcodes, execute flags divide-by-zero, memory flags page faults. The processor then prevents any writeback from flushed instructions and saves the PC of either the faulting instruction (for faults) or the following instruction (for traps). A concrete scenario: a divide-by-zero detected in execute causes the pipeline to flush the younger instructions that entered fetch and decode; any speculative register updates are prevented from reaching the architectural register file. A typical misconception is that only the fetch stage needs to be stalled; in truth, exceptions can originate in many stages, so detection and coordinated flush must be staged across the pipeline. The key is: the pipeline maintains the illusion of sequential execution by flushing or stalling until the precise exceptional state is restored and the handler completes.

Out-of-order processors execute instructions speculatively and complete them out of program order for performance. Because of this, exceptions cannot be handled by simply flushing later stages: some younger instructions may have finished execution earlier than older ones. The reorder buffer provides the mechanism for precise exceptions: it holds speculative results until instructions are committed in program order. If an exception occurs, the processor discards all uncommitted entries in the ROB and restores the architectural state to the last committed point, leaving the excepting instruction as the next to be handled. The ROB thus prevents speculative side effects from becoming visible before instructions are safe to commit. A concrete example: imagine instruction I causes a page fault while subsequent instructions J and K have already executed out of order and updated temporary buffers; the ROB ensures that I's fault will be presented to the OS while J and K's changes are not applied to the register file or memory. A common misconception is that out-of-order hardware cannot produce precise exceptions; in reality, the ROB is the hardware structure that preserves program-order commitments and enables precise recovery. The key takeaway: the ROB isolates speculation until commit, which is what allows correct exception semantics in aggressive cores.

Nested exceptions occur when a new exception arises while the processor is already executing an exception handler. To support nested exceptions the processor must save the handler's context as well — effectively stacking contexts so each level can be restored later. Implementations commonly use a dedicated exception stack or multiple banks of saved state to hold nested contexts. Most hardware supports only a limited number of nested levels to avoid exhausting resources; practical designs might allow two to four nested contexts. The OS and handlers must be written with this limit in mind: handlers typically run with minimal work, re-enable only safe interrupts if at all, and avoid deep recursion so that nested exception depth stays small. Consider this when designing robust handlers: minimize work in handlers, and plan for the limited nested context capacity.

When designing systems, reserve NMIs for truly urgent conditions and rely on maskable interrupts for normal device-driven work.

A few operational reminders round out the chapter. First, initialize the exception vector table early and ensure it contains privileged addresses; mistakes here can direct the C P U to invalid code. Second, design handlers to be minimal: save state, do essential work, and return with the privileged return instruction. Heavy work in handlers increases risk of nested exceptions and complicates recovery. Third, in virtualized environments decide which exceptions the hypervisor must intercept and which should be delivered to the guest; that mapping influences both performance and isolation. These practical rules will help you build correct, debuggable exception handling in processors and systems.
